entries.title: Whatever AI Safety Is, It’s Not This
entries.summary: Asking AI companies to self-regulate is a great way to pretend like you’ve accomplished something.
entries.content:
Here’s a fun history lesson for you. Don’t worry, we’ll make it quick! In 1966, nearly 51,000 people died on US highways. The overwhelming evidence suggested that many lives could have been saved with modern seat belts, which by then had been around for several years. The automotive industry responded by rallying together, and, in a triumph of self-regulation, voluntarily put the safety feature in every new vehicle that rolled off the line.

Kidding! Of course they didn’t do that. In the fall of 1966, Congress established the Department of Transportation and then passed the National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act as well as the Highway Safety Act, giving the federal government sweeping new authority to set safety standards. By 1968, seat belts were required in every new car. Despite a massive increase in highway traffic in the last 60 years, far fewer fatalities happen on the road today.

I was thinking about this while watching various AI CEOs huddle around US president Donald Trump on Tuesday, congratulating themselves and each other on having signed an AI safety accord. My colleague Maddy Varner wrote about the specific stipulations here, but the short version is that it’s largely up to the AI labs to keep themselves in check.

Or, as Trump put it even more succinctly in the Oval Office on Wednesday: “They’re gonna police, and they’re gonna police each other, and they’re gonna self-police, they’re gonna police themselves. It’s going to work out very well.”

So this is the current state of AI safety regulation. On one side are the AI executives, employees, and tech luminaries, who are all saying that there need to be clear, thoughtful, tactical rules introduced to avoid potential disaster. (Bill Gates, for instance, has been on a media blitz playing Cassandra about an AI apocalypse.) On the other side is Trump’s magical thinking that if you say something enough times, it must be true.

That’s not to say any of this is simple or easy. The question of how to properly “pace the frontier,” as some of those same executives like to say, remains open. Even if all of the major AI labs were to agree to a slowdown, there’s no good way to keep them to their word, and China would likely continue on its own path regardless. The US economy is increasingly propped up on the AI industry, which itself has become an ouroboros of financing deals and circular investments; any meaningful crackdown risks major instability that reaches well beyond Silicon Valley.

The automotive industry is also admittedly an imperfect analogy for all kinds of reasons. There’s no seat belt equivalent for AI, no straightforward solution that can demonstrably reduce risk overnight. (It also took decades for the majority of states to pass laws mandating that people actually wear them.) The potential harms are less certain and less quantifiable. AI doomers will tell you the technology could result in human extinction in a decade; skeptics argue that’s sci-fi marketing malarkey.

We’ve talked about various AI risk scenarios before, but no one can say for certain what’s going to happen next. If you’re looking for data points to calculate your own personal p(doom), I’d point to a recent CNN report about how the US military supposedly nearly boarded a Chinese ship in part because a false AI-generated report said it was carrying nuclear materials. What, if anything, does the AI accord accomplish to prevent similar incidents from happening in the future? Unclear.

The correct answer to all this uncertainty surely isn’t “I guess we’ll find out.” But that’s exactly what self-regulation encourages. To its credit, OpenAI has delayed and even canceled the release of its most advanced models over security concerns. But not before they went on various, extensive hacking sprees, new details about which are still trickling out at a steady pace.

In an interview with TIME published on Thursday, Trump suggested that the Department of Justice and the Federal Bureau of Investigation were sufficient “guardrails” for the artificial intelligence industry. Are they? It’s far from clear if AI companies can even be held legally responsible when their models go rogue. And it’s not like AI agents themselves are being served subpoenas.

The truth is, no one knows how to solve for AI safety right now. It’s going to take massive amounts of coordination, resources, and regulatory authority to develop the right framework and enforce it, which is exactly the kind of thing governments are designed to provide. Instead of even attempting to work through any of that, the Trump administration is getting out of the way and telling everyone to step on the gas. Don’t bother buckling up.

This is an edition of the Model Behavior newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

entries.title: The Best Early Prime Day Deals Ahead of Amazon’s Second Sale (2026)
entries.summary: Amazon Prime Big Deal Days officially begin on October 6 and 7, but I’ve already spotted early discounts on gear our team recommends.
entries.content:
Amazon Prime Day deals are back, baby. The second sale of the year is officially dubbed Prime Big Deal Days and will arrive on October 6 and 7. However, early deals have already started, and I've been using my 13 years of deal-hunting experience to find true discounts on the gadgets and gear the WIRED Reviews team has hand-tested and would recommend to our friends. Below, you'll find the best early deals we've sleuthed so far. We'll be covering deals throughout the event and beyond. all the way through Black Friday and Cyber Monday.

Don't miss our list of Prime Day tips put together by yours truly, plus our guide to Amazon Prime benefits you might be forgetting to use. Our guide to shopping safe on Amazon might be useful as well.

Updated October 1: We've added new deals from Amazon, De'Longhi, and Belkin. We've also checked prices and made sure existing deals are up to date.

  • The best earbuds deal: Google Pixel Buds Pro 2 for $190 ($41 off)
  • The best robot vacuum deal: Roborock Qrevo 2 Pro for $550 ($250 off)
  • A budget-friendly standing desk: FlexiSpot EN1 Standing Desk for $170 ($40 off)
  • The best Bluetooth speaker: JBL Flip 7 Bluetooth Speaker for $120 ($30 off)
  • An automatic espresso machine at an all-time low: De'Longhi Rivelia for $1,000 ($300 off)

Best Tech Deals

The JBL Go 5 is our top budget Bluetooth speaker. It's available in 10 different colors, most of which are down to a match of the best price we've seen. It's durable, lightweight, and sounds good for its size.

The Google Pixel Buds Pro 2 remain our top earbuds for Android users (they also work with iOS). They're aesthetically pleasing. They sound great. They're comfortable, have a long-lasting battery, and active noise cancellation, plus some useful software features. If you want good earbuds that aren't AirPods, these might be up your alley.

Amazon launched two new Echo Show smart displays last year, and the Echo Show 11 was easily the better of the two. This time around, the sound has been improved, and the screen is larger—but not so big that it's unwieldy to put in a kitchen counter. Amazon did raise the price $30 at the end of August, but this is still the lowest deal price I've seen for it since its launch, so it's still a good buy. —Nena Farrell

I have tested many, many Apple 3-in-1 wireless chargers, and it's worthy of a place on your nightstand. It's been redesigned, now using a classy-looking mix of matte zinc and soft-touch black plastic with a lovely weighted base. The iPhone pad can also be tilted to hold your iPhone vertically or horizontally, with support for StandBy mode. It can fast-charge iPhone and Apple Watch models, as well as charge any AirPods with a wireless charging case. The 5-foot barrel jack cable and 40-watt wall charger come bundled in the box. —Simon Hill

Best Home Deals

This is a really solid deal on the best automatic latte and cappuccino maker we've tested. The Rivelia is easy to use, and it even has a built-in milk frother in addition to the grinder. We also like the touchscreen display and consistently tasty results. This is an all-time low price, making it an ideal time to pick one up.—Louryn Strampe

The Roborock Qrevo 2 Pro is a solid, relatively affordable robot vacuum. It could do a better job at cleaning up tricky spills, but it has good suction power, and this is the best price we've seen since it was released.

Our top smart bird feeder is available in a few discounted configurations, but we prefer this one since it comes with AI bird identification and a solar charging panel. It's been slightly cheaper before, but this deal is still a good one.

I’ve tested air purifiers that cost 10 times as much as this budget Levoit, but I keep coming back to this affordable pick. I really love the connected app, which lets me adjust settings like fan speed and modes from afar and check filter life. Plus, the app sends notifications when air quality is poor and updates when it reaches clean levels again. You can also see historical indoor air quality levels and the corresponding action the purifier took, which helps track patterns. It’s also compatible with Amazon Alexa or Google Assistant for voice control. —Molly Higgins

One of the best cordless stick vacuums you can buy is available in a few different configurations, and one of those options is on sale. The Shark PowerDetect vacuum has powerful suction and a bendable body that can slide under furniture. The base station version comes with more features, and the Speed version is a little cheaper (and our current top pick), but only the sole PowerDetect vacuum is on sale as of press time. —Nena Farrell

Before it was an honorable mention in our router buying guide, the TP-Link Roam 7 was a top pick. And we still like it! It's a good portable option for traveling or smaller apartments, and it has support for mobile tethering and VPN.

entries.title: Trump’s ‘Morally Binding’ AI ‘Accord,’ the Rise of AI Agents, and Extremists on the Ballot
entries.summary: This week on “Uncanny Valley,” we discuss the voluntary AI safety agreement tech executives signed, AI agents for normies, and extremist candidates running for office in the US midterms.
entries.content:
This week on Uncanny Valley, Brian Barrett, Zoë Schiffer, and Leah Feiger discuss the “morally binding” AI accord tech executives signed following a meeting with Donald Trump. They’ve agreed that AI labs will regulate themselves—should work out great. Plus, the team digs into OpenAI’s Developer Day, where CEO Sam Altman introduced AI agents for normies, otherwise known as Dots; how AI agents are coming to workplaces near you; and a quick rundown of the most extremist candidates running for office.

Articles mentioned in this episode:

You can follow Brian Barrett on Bluesky at @brbarrett, Zoë Schiffer on Bluesky at @zoeschiffer, and Leah Feiger on Bluesky at @leahfeiger. Write to us at [email protected].

How to Listen

You can always listen to this week's podcast through the audio player on this page, but if you want to subscribe for free to get every episode, here's how:

If you're on an iPhone or iPad, open the app called Podcasts, or just tap this link. You can also download an app like Overcast or Pocket Casts and search for “uncanny valley.” We’re on Spotify too.

Transcript

Note: This is an automated transcript, which may contain errors.

Brian Barrett: Hey, this is Brian. Two quick things before we dive in. If you've been listening for a while and you haven't rated or reviewed the podcast yet, this is your sign. Give us a rating, tell us what you think. Five stars is nice, but we'll take the feedback too. It really helps more people find the show. Also, if you're in the Bay Area, we will be doing a live audience recording of the podcast on Thursday, October 8, at 7 pm at The Commons, headquarters of our KQED friends in San Francisco. You can buy tickets on kqed.org or check out the show notes for the link. You won't want to miss it. OK, onto the show.

Zoë Schiffer: Welcome to WIRED's Uncanny Valley. I'm Zoë Schiffer, contributing editor.

Brian Barrett: I'm Brian Barrett, executive editor.

Leah Feiger: And I'm Leah Feiger, director of politics and science.

Brian Barrett: This week we've got a new proclamation or rather a "morally binding" AI accord from the White House. After a meeting between tech executives and Donald Trump, it basically says the AI labs are going to regulate themselves. Should work out great. Plus we'll talk about OpenAI's Developer Day, where CEO Sam Altman announced the company's new always-on AI agents for regular folks. More AI agents again, should work out great. Everything's working out great today.

Zoë Schiffer: Yeah. And as AI agents become way more popular in Silicon Valley and beyond, employers are pushing to have these agents harmoniously work alongside human employees. We'll get into how that process is actually going and what the chances are that we're all going to have to welcome some bot colleagues very soon.

Leah Feiger: And with the midterm elections closing in, we're going to be talking about some of the extreme candidates running for office. It's not just political candidates who feel emboldened to say whatever they want. It's also people who are currently or have been recently working for the government, including a retired army colonel turned Pentagon influencer who WIRED reported this week, posted plenty of praise for dictators and has a plan to strip the vote from anyone without kids.

Brian Barrett: Let's start though with a nice luncheon that happened on Tuesday. President Trump invited all his favorite AI executives over to the White House. He had Sundar Pichai, Elon Musk, Dario Amodei, Mark Zuckerberg, Jensen Huang, OpenAI President Greg Brockman, not OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, plus a lot of companies that I was less familiar with. It felt like a little bit of a motley crew in some ways, but that's neither here nor there. They came out with a signed document called the White House Accord on Super Intelligence. Super intelligence, of course, how the government is now referring to AI, artificial intelligence. But in this accord, the companies agree that they should put their models through four layers of controls and audits. That includes internal evaluations, letting an outside audit firm come in and make sure everything's OK, and having the company's own board review those audits. And it's all voluntary.

Leah Feiger: That remains the keyword here. When it ever comes to any sort of proposed regulation at all that we've seen thus far in the AI space when it comes to the White House, voluntary is the word. I don't know, is it so silly of me to be so hung up on this that none of this is real? This is all fake.

Zoë Schiffer: Yeah, I don't think we were expecting the Trump administration to come out with real regulations for AI companies. Their big thing is—

Leah Feiger: For sure.

Zoë Schiffer: AI growth. But yeah, I mean when they came out, Trump came out in front of the White House with all of the CEOs, their kind of takeaway message was like, "We got this. We take it seriously. Don't worry about it." And I think it was actually stated by someone there like, "We'll regulate each other. We're looking out for each other."

Leah Feiger: I mean, we have to talk about this one particular moment. It's been gathering all sorts of attention online, where Dario Amodei is sort of awkwardly pushed to the front of the microphone to share some words and Trump praises him saying "Whatever he says is OK," which is great. So here's what he said.

Archival audio: Can we just bring Dario to the front for a second?

Donald Trump, archival audio: Where's Dario?

Brian Barrett: He does not want to be in the front, at all.

Donald Trump, archival audio: Whatever he says is OK.

Archival audio: So I just want to hear from you after this big summit where you are today.

Dario Amodei, archival audio: Look, I mean I will say what I've always said, which is that AI has incredible benefits. I've talked about them ...

Leah Feiger: I have so many thoughts. The first of which is Mark Zuckerberg trying to have a side chat with Trump during that.

Zoë Schiffer: Mark Zuckerberg—

Leah Feiger: Just happy to be in the room.

Zoë Schiffer: —and Trump are just off to the side making faces with each other.

Leah Feiger: I mean, look, this was all clearly such a rushed job. I can't help but think this is just sort of a way to tell the American public a couple of weeks ahead of midterms, "Don't worry, we have the regulation situation under control. Here are the richest, most powerful men in the country lined up telling you we're going to regulate it. It's all good. We're aware this is not doing well with polls right now, but we've got this." It just feels like a grab bag. Which perhaps is most emphasized by the fact that the words US were quite literally misspelled in the accords document. It reads President of the Unites States under Trump's signature, which is, I don't know, I'm not saying they quickly rushed this together, slap dash, signed it on, flew people out, but I'm not saying it doesn't look like they didn't do that either.

Brian Barrett: Can I say one thing that is weird about this to me? Or not weird, but the AI labs are in such an uncomfortable position, not that I have that much sympathy for them, but they want some meaningful regulatory framework because they're worried about being investigated for antitrust if they don't have some sort of go ahead to slow down, all this. But then the day after, so on Tuesday they have, hey, here's this framework. Everything's going to be fine. Y'all self-regulate. And then on Wednesday, the FTC says that they are ramping up a big probe of Anthropic and OpenAI and other frontier labs about the dangers that their technology poses to consumers. So you're sort of getting it from both sides from the government.

Zoë Schiffer: Yeah. And we have Lina Khan writing an op-ed in the New York Times today saying they actually can be tried under existing laws. We don't necessarily need to make new laws, with the big caveat that Congress would have to act.

Leah Feiger: And senior political correspondent Hugo Lowell for his newsletter this week for WIRED also wrote about how team Trump is very aware that the polls are not in their favor. It does not look like they're going to be winning Congress. And as a result, they're starting to look ahead into the future and to how to avoid all of these subpoenas and investigations the Democrats are sure to slap them with. So with that in mind, I have no doubt that you are right, Brian. Everyone's kind of looking at this going, okay, this is our moment right now, but what is this going to look for us, not even just in a couple of years when Trump's out of office, but in a couple of months when Democrats ostensibly are going to control the House and Senate.

Zoë Schiffer: I personally think Republicans are going to do great in the midterms, but you can cut that because I am not reporting on politics and that's just my vibe check.

Leah Feiger: I'm changing my mind constantly. Right now, I think that with gas prices the way that they are and certain polls coming back the way that they are, it will be really surprising to me if the Democrats manage to lose this. Not Republicans win this, this would require the Democrats messing up, which again, all possible.

Zoë Schiffer: Going back to the AI summit and luncheon, Brian, were you or were you not surprised to see not a hint of an Apple representative?

Brian Barrett: A little bit. Apple has been, they were the ones who memorably Tim Cook presented Donald Trump with a golden trinket.

Zoë Schiffer: Apparently not big enough.

Brian Barrett: No big enough. Not a big enough trinket. Do you read it, Zoë and Leah, as Apple just not being relevant enough in AI still today?

Zoë Schiffer: 100%.

Brian Barrett: I think they would be there in a heartbeat if they were invited.

Zoë Schiffer: It's not that they were bad at diplomacy.

Leah Feiger: But is Mark Zuckerberg that relevant?

Brian Barrett: Yes. 100%.

Zoë Schiffer: Yeah.

Leah Feiger: You think? OK. All right, I'm wrong.

Brian Barrett: Meta has the most popular consumer AI agent today.

Zoë Schiffer: Not because the AI agent ... They just have distribution and so Meta's AI can be so popular so fast because they can shove it down everyone's throats and that's exactly what they're doing. And they're basically promoting a free AI agent that they're subsidizing pretty heavily at the moment. And so yeah, but I think Apple is just frankly not in the game. Not in the game.

Brian Barrett: Talking of AI agents and Muse is what we're talking about. Meta's Muse AI agent has taken the app store by storm, but that's because it hasn't had much competition until on Tuesday, as we said, OpenAI had its Dev Day. And in his big keynote speech, Sam Altman walked on stage and devoted most of his time to Dots, which is OpenAI's answer to Muse. It's their always-on agents. You can interact with them through ChatGPT or Slack. The features are pretty established at this point. You can basically tell your agent to go do whatever task online for you and they will get it done. Zoë, I know, has been playing around with her own agents. You're much deeper into that than Leah and I are. Two things here. One, how much does OpenAI need Dots to connect in order to maintain its position in the AI race? And two, how'd they do in terms of adorability? They're really going for adorability, they're trying to make them adorable, I don't think they quite connected. I think Muse is cuter. There, I said. It doesn't mean you should use either of them.

Zoë Schiffer: This is a conversation?

Brian Barrett: It is though. So I'm talking over you because—

Zoë Schiffer: No, no, do it.

Brian Barrett: I'm joking, but the whole point of I think the fact that they're making these so cutesy and fluffy and adorable is obviously intentional. It is what is going to win over the average consumer and make you forget that you are giving away all of your privacy and all of the information and all of your accounts to this adorable fuzzy-wuzzy little thing instead of a data center.

Leah Feiger: Is that part of internet safety conversations now, Brian? When you sit around with your kids and you're like, you're going to have access to this, don't be fooled by the fuzzy avatar. They just want your bank details.

Brian Barrett: Yeah, I think don't hang out with fuzzy avatars online is a well-established directive for children.

Leah Feiger: Brian's rules for the road folks. You've heard it here.

Brian Barrett: Yeah.

Zoë Schiffer: Yeah. Well, I was just going to say, I was at the Developer Day yesterday, and I had a few observations. On one hand, OpenAI does seem really focused right now. I heard from people at the company that they shipped Dots, these kind of cute, fuzzy, always-on agents within a matter of weeks. They saw Instinct and Muse, these other kind of OpenClaw for normie-type agents and were like, "OK, we have to play this game." And they got it together really, really fast. I think it's interesting because a lot of these capabilities have actually existed for a minute now, but when you talk to people in the industry, they'll talk about form factor a lot. The new agents have to download a new app or learn new tools, and they're actually proactively learning about your life and then suggesting things they can do for you versus you seeing this blank text box and being like, “I can build anything. What would I want to build,” is actually a big difference. I was really struck yesterday thinking, "Wow, Anthropic is on the back foot," which hasn't happened a lot recently. And they, I think, really do need to ship something interesting in this space sooner rather than later. But like you both said, there's just this constant tension and trade-off, which is to make these agents useful, you have to give them a lot of personal information. Otherwise, they just can't frankly do that much. And to give them that much personal information, you're taking a risk. It's totally reasonable to decide you don't want to go that route. Dots gets access to your email, your calendar, sometimes your financial information, and then it can do things on your behalf. The kind of gateway drug, if you talk to people who use these, and I'm one of them, is restaurant reservations. You can say, "Hey, I'm going to New York at this time. Can you book these tables for me?" And it'll wait for when the reservation block opens and it'll book you a table. I was actually, I have to say, Noah Shinn, who's the CEO of Instinct, he's 23 years old. I repeat, this man is 23 years old. His company, less than two years old, valued at $10 billion now. He gave his first longform interview since his app completely blew up, and he talked about restaurant reservations. I was really waiting to be like, "This man has thought deeply about what happens to the internet when agents are doing all of your browsing and booking." No, sir. No. Mm-mm. He was like, "It's going to be great because previously restaurant reservations were first come first serve, and now your agent can say if it's your birthday or an anniversary and then the restaurant can prioritize you." I was like, "You only have to think about this for two seconds to realize that then everyone will just say it's their anniversary or birthday. What do you mean?" Anyway.

Leah Feiger: Oh, my God, I'm so depressed.

Brian Barrett: It's funny, that reminds me of, we're getting a little bit off topic, but another in that same vein, there was a warning this week from one of the banks, I believe, or just sort of an observation that as everyone gets these agents, they're always going to be optimizing and they're always going to be looking for the best result for their user. And we're not set up in a world where everybody's optimizing all the time. The example they gave was banking. If everyone takes all of their money from low to no interest rate savings accounts and puts them all into money market accounts where they're making 3% to 6%, whatever, on that account, the US financial system could collapse basically. It's like a run on the bank, because we are built for, that system is built on assuming that people are going to have very low to no interest rates because that's how banks can make their own interest on it. So yeah, when we have this world where everybody has their own AI agent looking out for their best interests, negotiating with other AI agents to figure out who gets the best result, I think we're going to run into some really interesting unintended consequences.

Zoë Schiffer: For sure. And the other thing that I was really struck by yesterday, going back to Leah's point, is it just felt like there were a lot of different messages being said about what an agent like Dot can do. It's like this cute, fuzzy agent, except they kind of brushed away the restaurant reservation thing. It was like, of course they can book tables for you, but it can also do all of this hardcore engineering bug bashing stuff. And mentioned security and privacy, I do think this is something they're thinking about, but it just feels like the messaging around them is really confused. Ben Thompson talked about this recently on TBPN, and he was like, "Most people don't want to be more productive. They want other things. You shop because shopping's entertaining." This idea that we're all builders and we all want to optimize every area of our life, do more work, I don't think speaks to a lot of people.

Leah Feiger: I think that's the thing that I keep coming back to. Even with the restaurant reservation world, and look, this isn't for everyone, but you say to an agent, "I want to go to three of the best restaurants in New York City that will be priced under 150 a person." That's a very specific liminal space. Obviously, I get it. If you don't have a lot of time, you have a work trip, you have whatever. There's a lot of people who really enjoy reading the New York Times best restaurant reviews and combing through the blogs and this is where this person I really trust has told me that I should go. So the idea of optimizing everything also feels like then we lose so much, right?

Zoë Schiffer: Totally.

Leah Feiger: And again, I get that it's not for everyone. No everyone has the same interest here, but there is this very weird missing piece, missing cultural piece that all of a sudden goes.

Zoë Schiffer: Yeah. The other thing that Noah Shinn, again, the CEO of Instinct, talked about on that podcast when the interviewer, who again is setting up a pretty slam dunk interview, these questions were not super hard-hitting, but he's like, "What are you excited about?" He named the restaurant reservation thing. And then he's like, "Also, people are taking photos of every item in their closet and then Instinct is suggesting outfits for their week." And I was like, obviously, I'm not the core demographic here, but you think an agent built by a 23-year-old engineer is going to give you sartorial advice that you actually want to follow?

Leah Feiger: Again, it's the what culture are we losing people? I find a new argument every week for something making me mad, and that might be it today.

Brian Barrett: Well, I'll say not only that, not only is there the question of how many people really want these? And to be clear, maybe everyone wants these. Maybe these could be huge, a lot of people are enjoying their Muse.

Leah Feiger: I mean, not everyone is against this. Zoë, not to call you out, you want this life. You want the robot command center.

Zoë Schiffer: Yeah. I mean, I'm using the agents, and this is what is interesting to me, is I do think that they are useful and valuable. Last night, Andrew asked me when a babysitter was coming next week, and I had the agent put together a shared calendar, a child care calendar with the dates that the girls don't have school, the dates we have coverage, the dates we need coverage, share it with everyone relevant. That would've taken me an hour and it happens in less than a minute. It is really nice. Of course, to make that happen, you have to have an agent have calendar access, access to your email, be able to share a calendar with other people in your email. Again, these are all risks. But what's interesting to me is when you hear the AI executives talk about the technology and the possibility of the technology, to me, it feels like they don't even get what they're building. I don't know a lot of people, and certainly I don't want this, that want an AI agent to give them fashion advice. The stuff that they want, that I want is really basic and mundane.

Leah Feiger: You want an assistant.

Zoë Schiffer: Yeah, because the agents can do so much more, they're like, "Well, yeah, of course it can do that, but here are all these other things." But people actually just want the basic things done and done reliably and well and without putting all their information at risk, and we need to nail that in order for this to really go mainstream.

Leah Feiger: Do you have fears? OK. Yeah, I'm just so curious because in so many ways me not doing this is not because I decry the usefulness. Honestly, like you describing a shared family calendar, I'm like, "I need that. I need that yesterday and I just haven't gotten around to it," but I haven't done it because I'm scared, full stop. I'm just actively scared. How do you manage that?

Zoë Schiffer: I mean, I am scared. I talked about this in the article I wrote about Instinct last week. I live in fear of my personal information getting out, getting beyond my control, all of that stuff. And I think I'm more scared now with agents than I was before, for sure. At the same time, the agents can be useful for, the other week, a friend sent out a paperless post for a barbecue. My dad clicked on it. I was instantly warned by my agent that it was a phishing scam, and so I didn't. And so my kind of read was, I'm really busy. I could make a mistake just myself going around my life because I'm trying to multitask and pick the girls up from school while I'm working and all of this stuff. And so it's helpful having another set of eyes. The fact that set of eyes could then be its own security risk sucks. I think about that all the time, but right now I'm willing to take the risk, because I am finding value from them and that might change.

Brian Barrett: Zoë, right now, you are making a personal choice to use an AI agent in your life, which is great. Increasingly though, people don't have that choice, right? The AI agent coworkers are becoming increasingly the norm. WIRED senior writer Kate Taylor reported on it this week. How do you feel about AI agents in the workplace, Zoë, pinging you on Slack?

Zoë Schiffer: Yeah, so this was actually something that OpenAI talked about at their Developer Day. They had an OpenAI employee come up and demo how she uses her Dot, I think the name was Dottie, as kind of a colleague. She can add it on Slack. She can mention it in documents and it can respond and go back and forth. Obviously, that's someone who is actively choosing to do that. I think having an agent forced on you is different, honestly. I mean, sorry if this is the dumbest take, but I'm like, it all comes down to how good the agent is. We've all had the experience of having to talk to a robot on a customer service call and having it be so frustrating because it just cannot understand what you're saying and you're just dying to talk to a human. If that call worked, I don't know if you'd be sitting there being like, "Oh, this is a tragic situation." You would still understand the job loss and the misfortune of that, but you personally wouldn't necessarily be completely aggravated.

Brian Barrett: One thing that was interesting to me in Kate's story was there seems to be, and it makes sense, a difference of opinion about how much you anthropomorphize. Do you have an agent coworker who you treat like a human and you have that kind of casual conversation that represents as such? Or is it a tool and you treat it like a tool and you don't give it a human name, you just sort of know that it's there doing the work for you? There's a real divide there in terms of what role they should play, how you should treat them, how you deal with them in this environment, these agents.

Leah Feiger: Oh, that freaked me out. I mean, the fact that that's the thing, that's what they're trying to do here.

Zoë Schiffer: Yeah, I mean, I feel like that is a question that has existed since OpenAI launched ChatGPT in 2022. The thing that LLMs can do is talk to you with natural language, is sound more human than a traditional bot. And I think that the company saw really, really quickly that from their point of view, this was a feature, not a bug. People liked interacting with something that felt more human. And you can see in these specific circumstances with apps that are used to tutor kids, it's helpful ... A good human tutor isn't just throwing math problems at you. It's also saying, "You're doing really good." It's being a little bit encouraging, and so it can be helpful if the app is doing that. The flip side of that is that you can forget that what you're talking to is a system, it's software, and we've seen, obviously, people get really attached to these systems. They form relationships with these systems.

Leah Feiger: I was also really struck though in the article about the risk of dehumanizing. It's not just these very, I'm sorry, bizarre parasocial attachments to not human colleagues. It's the risk that humanizing these AI agents actually really lowers everyone's guard to catching mistakes and actually doing your job. Kate cited that BCG Research found that managers caught 18% fewer errors when told work came from an AI employee versus an AI tool, which is a fascinating difference.

Zoë Schiffer: Can I say something that's kind of vaguely related, but a little bit of a pivot? I installed the Pangram extension on Chrome, and so now I can click any webpage and see how much of it is AI generated, and I have been testing myself with Substack and some of the more longform newsletters that I read. I can tell the moment that it switches. It's like, I'm interested, I'm interested, and then my eyes start to glaze over and I'm like, God, am I not able to focus? And I'll look and it's like, no, the AI generated stuff just starts to get so verbose. It's so long. It loves bullet points so much. These tools are not an excuse to just output bad work. And if it's taking you less time to create the work than someone has to take to consume it, if that makes sense, I think that that's a huge problem.

Leah Feiger: To me, the framing is, is it an assistant or is it a colleague? I think that hierarchy is really important here.

Zoë Schiffer: Mm-hmm.

Brian Barrett: And I do think that's the difference between having ChatGPT integrations all over your workspace and having AI agents in your workspace. It's a fundamentally different thing that's happening now. I think it's a tool at best, but I don't know. I think in five years, maybe we'll have a fourth cohost of this podcast.

Zoë Schiffer: Podcast host. Oh my God.

Leah Feiger: Oh, that's—

Brian Barrett: Dottie.

Leah Feiger: It won't be a fourth because if it is, I'm out, to be entirely clear. Welcome, Dottie. I bid adieu. I'm wrenching this back into the political realm. Is that OK with you guys?

Zoë Schiffer: Yeah.

Brian Barrett: Do it.

Leah Feiger: All right. We have five weeks left until the midterms. I'm so excited. Primaries are over, candidates are running. It's all very official. People are spending money. We have so much to say about all of this, but for this episode, I want to talk about some of the very specific candidates. Obviously, there's a couple of national races that have gotten a lot of attention, but I want to talk about some that really haven't, more specifically, candidates that are extremist or have espoused extremist views or employ extremist colleagues. It's a very open tent, I would say. But again, there's this massive subset of candidates that are in the running despite all of these controversies. WIRED reporter David Gilbert reviewed many of these candidates running for statewide and federal positions in November, found hundreds of Republican candidates espousing all sorts of hateful ideologies. They share racist comments online, have close ties to white supremacists who are antisemitic figures, members of far-right online groups, over 500 candidates specifically running for state legislature positions in November, and I want to talk to you guys about them. Who caught your attention? Who should we talk about first?

Brian Barrett: Why don't we start with my favorite, a race that I care deeply about, Texas Railroad Commissioner.

Leah Feiger: Good. Bo French.

Brian Barrett: I was following this one even before. We got Bo French, GOP candidate. Leah, tell us about Bo French.

Leah Feiger: Oh, I mean, this man is so extreme that Republican strategist Carl Rove has said he would vote for a Democrat rather than support a "bigot." He is currently a slim favorite to win the seat. And if that Carl Rove indictment doesn't get you, I'm not 100% sure what will. But a couple of other anecdotes is earlier this month, French posted racist comments about students of South Asian descent celebrating University of Texas Austin football victory over Ohio State, said some terrible stuff about "foreigners." There's no, we found bad tweets of his when he was in high school. This is currently happening. And to get back to this position that he's running for, Texas Railroad Commissioner does sound like a position on a monopoly board game, but it's actually really important. Doesn't have any role in regulating railroads. It actually oversees the state's oil and gas industries, which drill more oil and hydrocarbons than the rest of the US combined. Especially as we are in this era of data centers and AI growth, this is an important position in a really important state that also has other key races happening that'll determine the flipping of the House and Senate. So I'm fascinated by the Bo French controversy of all.

Zoë Schiffer: I think it'll be really interesting because one thing that I've noticed when listening to Republicans talk about this is that the ones that are against people like Bo French say it's bad for the party. Having these views is not good for Republicans. I think if people start winning these races, I'm curious how that flips. If it doesn't look like it's bad for the party, how that changes things.

Leah Feiger: I mean, people who have espoused not dissimilar views have held even higher positions of power. And so in some ways, it's like a ton of extremists are running for office, and perhaps the notable part of this is a ton of extremists are running for office again. They were validated in the last several elections. We are in a different era of American politics. The thing that I keep coming back to is it's really not hard to find dirt on people. We were going through fact check for this article and our wonderful research team is like, "Where did you find this? Where is this?" And David's just like, "Here's the X post, here's the Facebook post." It's right there. This was a week ago," which is a wild thing.

Brian Barrett: Two of the things that really got me with this story. One, when I heard we were doing the story and we talked about it beforehand, I was assuming, wow, there's going to be dozens of extremist candidates, but there are hundreds and hundreds, 500 just for state legislatures alone. And then the other thing is how many of these people are probably going to win. Not all of them. Some of them already lost the primaries, but a surprising and disappointing number of these people are going to come out ahead, including a Senate candidate, Georgia Senate, Mike Collins, running pretty close, is it fair to say, against Jon Ossoff and has a lot of ties that are concerning to people who are close to white supremacy, antisemitism, pretty rough stuff.

Leah Feiger: I want to talk about this other race as well. It's also in Texas. It's Texas's 23rd congressional district race. Trump has recently endorsed Brandon Herrera, the GOP candidate. He rose to fame as a so-called gun tuber, aka a lot of gun talk on YouTube. I hate that there's a name for it. He's running for Congress in Texas in the district that represents Uvalde. Herrera has an incredibly long history of very, very openly sharing virulently sexist, racist, antisemitic opinions. He said that the Nazi era submachine gun was the original "ghetto blaster," "Hitler's street sweeper," has said really horrible stuff about activists who are part of Moms Demand Action that I honestly don't really want to say out loud. Go to the article for more, but really, really gross stuff. Trump in March wrote, "He will never let you down." This isn't fringe. I think that's the thing that I want to get back to here is that these are not actually fringe candidates. Herrera's in a tight race with the Democratic nominee, Katy Padilla, but there is this, I think a wild notion of the word extreme, to me at least, has lost a little bit of meaning. But these aren't very extremist viewpoints to your point, Brian, in so many of these races at this moment.

Zoë Schiffer: I mean, yeah, I think it's important that we still continue to use that word, because even though the views are getting more widely adopted, it is important to say that. Again, the reason this is, to me, so shocking is Uvalde is the site of a horrific mass shooting that took place at a school with really young children not that long ago.

Leah Feiger: Right. Right. While all of these candidates, we're going to see how it goes for them in November, I'm sure that I'll be back to tell you details from David Gilbert. But we also reported this week on a man with not dissimilar views who has been working in government, specifically with the Pentagon. You may have seen this a couple of weeks ago, I was very obsessed with this story. The Washington Post broke it and they were looking into the Pentagon's employment of influencers in civilian roles, very specifically employment of. So we're talking people who are supposed to be in support of Secretary Pete Hegseth's de-wokifying the military plan, but they're actually working for the government. So the Washington Post named this man, Kurt Schlichter, a retired army colonel turned social media influencer, as one of these people. They did not report on anything else that he has said, which was a bummer for them, but a boon for us because he has said insane things. This guy has over 600,000 followers on X. David Gilbert found and reported that his social media posts included exactly what you think they did, inflammatory, racist, misogynistic statements, including probably my favorite quote of all, which is calling liberal women a "pestilence, a plague upon Western society." I thought that was unique at the very least. I get a lot of mean emails all the time. I've never been called a pestilence. I might reply if you say that to me in an email from here on out. This was in a July 2026 article for the conservative website Town Hall where he said those things. This person was brought into the government. According to the post, he appeared in the government database with a designation HQE, which could stand for highly qualified expert. These kinds of things have been surfacing for years, but it's still, every single time, it gets me.

Zoë Schiffer: Yeah, I feel like, I mean, it's good to be surprised and at the same time, I'm not entirely surprised because so much of the current culture feels like a backlash to "cancel culture," this idea that you could say something online and then you'd have stuff taken away from you supposedly. Now I feel like, especially in the current administration, the current Trump administration, their stance is like, no, no, no. If you support the president, if you support the Trump administration, you can say a whole lot of things and you're still part of the party.

Brian Barrett: Yeah, and if anything, you are encouraged to say them. That same rhetoric also got him to the hundreds of thousands of followers in the first place. Leah, is it fair to say that people like Schlichter wind up in the White House, not in spite of comments that they've made in the past, but because of comments that they've made in the past?

Leah Feiger: Yeah, absolutely. I mean, these are comments that are being echoed or championed by the commander-in-chief. What we're going to see is I'm watching as polling is coming out for the midterms. For example, governor of Texas, Ken Paxton, who's running for Senate in Texas against James Talarico, he has apparently, according to reporting from the New York Times, come out and said that associating with Trump really hasn't been the best for him so far. That is starting to come out slowly. I've heard that from a number of other people, from a number of other consultants. To me, I then wonder what's the next step of that? Do you then kind of stop espousing similar extremist views? Was it all for the polling? Was it all to get you into these positions? I think we're going to see a very interesting switch because regardless of what happens in the midterms in the coming weeks, by early next year, Donald Trump is going to be a lame duck president.

Zoë Schiffer: Coming up after the break, we're sharing our WIRED/TIRED picks for the week. Stay with us.

Leah Feiger: It is time for our WIRED/TIRED segment. Whatever is new and cool is WIRED and whatever passé thing we're over is TIRED. Brian, do you want to go first?

Brian Barrett: I do, and I know I have a reputation here of caring more about consumer tech certainly than you two do, and maybe than I should, but it's important. So here's my WIRED. My WIRED, not intentionally, is a literal wired thing. Bose this week announced its first wired headphones in years. Everything has been Bluetooth. Everything is Bluetooth all the time. Bose, makes very good headphones, they have introduced wired headphones for a couple of reasons. One, because apparently teens really want them because they're tired of Bluetooth. But two, it's just nice to have the option of plugging something in and not worrying if the Bluetooth is connecting and not worrying about are my headphones charged? It hearkens back to simpler times of headphones. So I am glad that we are giving people the option to plug things in instead of relying on Bluetooth and battery-powered devices. That's my WIRED. My TIRED, we talked about Kate Taylor earlier, terrific senior writer at WIRED. Last week for a different story than the one we talked about, Kate actually made AI bots of me and senior editor Sophie Kleeman and interacted with them for several weeks to a month. I hated it. I hated having a Brian Bot, made me very uncomfortable. Don't make Brian Bots. They're bad. They're TIRED.

Leah Feiger: But read the article because it's very good.

Brian Barrett: But do read the article, it's a great article, but forget everything about the Brian Bot part.

Leah Feiger: Zoë, what are yours?

Zoë Schiffer: Okay. My TIRED is AI leaders who are being paid hundreds of millions, possibly billions of dollars, posting whatever jokey, lame, sexual stuff on X all throughout the day and night. I am talking here specifically about Alexandr Wang, head of AI at Meta, head of Meta Super Intelligence Labs. He has been posting incessantly about how OpenAI's logo looks like a butthole. He's been posting, "Do you get turned on when you look at the fluffy Muse logo?" I just am like, "Sir, this stuff is actually serious and you do not appear to be a serious person in any way whatsoever." Thus, WIRED is like, sorry, corporate communications. He has said like, "Oh, I don't let those corporate hacks anywhere near my Twitter account." And I think you should. I think you should have them run it, because right now you're embarrassing everyone, including yourself.

Leah Feiger: That's really good.

Zoë Schiffer: Thank you.

Leah Feiger: Wait, is that your TIRED?

Zoë Schiffer: That was both My TIRED and my WIRED.

Leah Feiger: And your WIRED. OK. That actually perfectly relates to mine, which is an article that was written by WIRED's Elana Klein a couple of days ago titled "Why No One Wants to Date Tech Bros." Every couple, I don't know, every couple of weeks, every couple of months, depending on the season, I have group chats that will be like, "Oh, this WIRED article has made it out of containment. Everyone is sending it to me. Who wrote this? This is so funny. What's the backstory?" Et cetera, et cetera. That story of this week was "Why No One Wants to Date Tech Bros." It's an excellent tale about people watching the turn. We're watching the turn against tech bro culture in the larger cultural landscape. I lived for it. I loved it. I highly recommend this read. It's a really good one. That is, I suppose, my combination of WIRED and TIRED, which is yeah, rough.

Zoë Schiffer: It's really good that I am married because I do identify as a tech bro and I just wouldn't want to live through this current backlash.

Leah Feiger: I mean, when I talk about having one, one tech bro friend, it's you. That's who I'm referring to.

Zoë Schiffer: Thank you.

Brian Barrett: And thank you for excluding me from that too.

Zoë Schiffer: Brian Bot, tech bro. Brian, not a tech bro.

Leah Feiger: Exactly. That's our show for today. I want to remind you that you can listen to this show along with our weekly download as well as audio versions of WIRED articles on the WIRED app. You can even curate playlists and share content. So check out The WIRED app. This episode was produced by Kate Osborn and Adriana Tapia, mixed by Kyle Murdoch. Our studio engineer was Vince Fairchild, fact checking by Matt Giles. Our global editorial director is Katie Drummond.

entries.title: Tim Heidecker Is Bringing His Joe Rogan Parody Show to The Onion
entries.summary: Five years after the comedian went viral with a 12-hour blabberthon mocking the king of bro podcasting, he’s back in character to shill a supplement called “Crab Salts.”
entries.content:
As satirical news outlet The Onion continued to wage a legal battle to acquire the assets of Infowars out of bankruptcy this summer, it launched a streaming program that spoofed the brand and its bellowing conspiracist ringleader, Alex Jones.

Comedian Tim Heidecker took the reins of the operation, adopting Jones’ guttural and paranoid bluster as he investigated, among other unconfirmed reports, whether Jones himself had exploded in his car after eating too much Whataburger.

But Heidecker wasn’t about to stop there in his quest to transform the Infowars brand into a gonzo comedy network along the lines of Adult Swim. Now he’s taking aim at another high-profile target: Joe Rogan, the bro podcaster whose rambling, misinformed conversations with everyone from Vice President JD Vance to [checks notes] Yakov Smirnoff have somehow kept his long-running series, The Joe Rogan Experience, at the top of the charts for years. Heidecker’s companion show, The Tim Heidecker Podcast, premieres at 8 pm ET on Thursday night, and WIRED can exclusively reveal that the debut episode includes lots of complaining about pronouns, wildly dumb speculation around AI, and plugs for a supplement called “Crab Salts” that makes your “head hurt” and causes you to shout.

A representative for Rogan did not immediately return a request for comment.

Heidecker first lampooned Rogan’s discursive and disorganized interviews in 2021, with a viral 12-hour podcast (in reality, one hour of footage looped a dozen times) covering topics including psychedelics, cancel culture, and whether Dwayne “The Rock” Johnson would run for president. His guests for that show, comedy duo and Onion contributors Rajat Suresh and Jeremy Levick, return for the new episode, offering their “expert” takes on hot-button topics. (The pair have essentially perfected the art of fake celebrity web content and once even got Justin Theroux in on the joke for a mock Hollywood Reporter-style actors roundtable.)

“What is essentially happening is, in place of Christianity, we have the 10 commandments of woke,” Levick says during a discussion of DEI policies on the first episode of The Tim Heidecker Podcast. The chat veers into concerns that bearded men are dressing as princesses to visit Disneyland. Heidecker then abruptly informs the boys that he’s planned a weekend trip to Glasgow “for Scotch wrestling.”

In 2026, it’s more difficult than ever to exaggerate the absurdities of the right-wing media ecosystem, with its fact-free moral panics and bizarre alternative medicines. Though if anyone is up to the task, it’s the endlessly inventive Heidecker—who will have no shortage of grifters and lunatics to go after once he’s done with his run as a Rogan type. Luckily for him, few of those potential impressions are as rough on the voice as Alex Jones.

entries.title: What’s the Best Kindle of 2026 (So Far)?
entries.summary: I’ve tested every single Kindle. Here’s how Amazon’s ebook readers stack up.
entries.content:
Featured in this article

There’s a lot to love about a Kindle if you’re a reader. If you’re looking for the best Kindle, you really can’t go wrong with any of the models. These Amazon-powered ebook readers let you bring thousands of books anywhere and typically give a month of battery life per charge. You can subscribe to get unlimited books from Amazon or get free books from your local library. Our guide will help you decode the differences to find which Kindle is right for you.

I've owned all kinds of Kindles, from the newest Kindle Scribes to hand-me-down base Kindles without a front light. The latter came from a friend who noticed I had spent my entire postpartum summer glued to library books on my phone, and I still have it to this day. But after trying all of the latest Kindles, I can say it's easy to spot the best one.

Read on to find out my favorite overall Kindle and my favorite Kindles for specific uses and younger readers. You can also check out my other buying guides made for readers like me, including the Best Kindle Accessories, Best E-Readers, Best Digital Notebooks, and Best Gifts for Book Lovers.

Updated October 2026: I've added details about the new Kindles announced today.

Comparing Our Favorite Kindles

Model Display Resolution Color? Storage Weight Battery life Waterproof
Kindle Paperwhite (2024, 12th Gen) 7 inches, adjustable warm light 300 pixels per inch (ppi) No 16 GB 7.4 ounces Up to 12 weeks Yes, IPX8
Kindle Scribe (2024, 2nd Gen) 10.2 inches, adjustable warm light, auto-adjusting front light 300 ppi No 16, 32, or 64 GB 15.3 ounces Up to 12 weeks No
Kindle Colorsoft (2025) 7 inches, adjustable warm light 300 ppi (Black-and-White), 150 ppi (Color) Yes 16 GB 7.6 ounces Up to 8 weeks Yes, IPX8
Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition (2024) 7 inches, adjustable warm light, auto-adjusting front light 300 ppi (B&W), 150 ppi (Color) Yes 32 GB 7.7 ounces Up to 8 weeks Yes, IPX8
Kindle Colorsoft Kids (2025) 7 inches, adjustable warm light 300 ppi (B&W), 150 ppi (Color) Yes 16 GB 11.8 ounces Up to 8 weeks Yes, IPX8
Kindle (2024, 11th Gen) 6 inches, adjustable front light 300 ppi No 16 GB 5.56 ounces Up to 6 weeks No

What Are the New Kindles?

Amazon announced today that there's a whole new generation of Kindles coming, with every model getting a new version. Here are the details; I'll be updating this guide soon with thoughts as we review each model.

  • Kindle (2026, 12th Generation) for $150: This is the new version of the base Kindle, with many features that will sound familiar (a 6-inch screen, six weeks of battery life, and 16 GB of storage) but a new flush-front design for the screen and lighter weight. It maintains the new $150 price tag that the older base Kindle just moved to in August. You can also choose the Aluminum version that has a more premium feel and different colors, plus 32 GB of storage. Both versions are available now.
  • Kindle Paperwhite (2026, 13th Generation) for $200: The 2026 Kindle Paperwhite will still pack a waterproof design and 12 weeks of battery life (my favorite part!), but now promises an updated display with the largest Kindle Paperwhite screen yet and a higher contrast ratio. The Signature Edition will now have aluminum backing, and also pack dock charging with pogo pins on the back and a double tap to turn pages. The regular Paperwhite is available for preorder and retails for $200 (same as the old model) with 16 GB of storage and comes in only black, while the Paperwhite Signature Edition is also on preorder for $250 and comes in two colors with 32 GB of storage. The preorder is available on a rolling basis in various regions, so it might not be available in yours right away.
  • Kindle Colorsoft (2026, 2nd Generation) for $290: The Kindle Colorsoft gets a second-generation model with an updated display and edge-to-edge color, and promises richer color than the first generation. It gets a similar new flush-front design to the other Kindle models, and also comes in a Signature Edition that has aluminum backing, an auto-adjusting front light, pogo points for charging, and the double-tap to turn pages. The new Colorsoft is available for preorder at $290 and with 16 GB of storage, while the new Colorsoft Signature Edition is also on preorder for $320 with 32 GB of storage and two device colors to choose from. Similar to the Paperwhite, the preorders are rolling out to various regions, so keep an eye out if it's not available for you yet.
  • Kindle Kids models starting at $180: All three of the above models will have a Kids version that will include kid-friendly covers and 12 months of Amazon Kids+ content. The base Kindle Kids is available now, while others are on preorder in certain regions.

That's not all Kindle has coming out. There will also be a handful of new accessories, including the Kindle Click ($35) Bluetooth remote that will work with Kindle models as early as 2024, a Page-Turn Cover ($80), a Charging Dock ($60) designed to work with the pogo pins on the Signature Editions, and new Kindle covers in a variety of colors and textures. I'm most excited about the remote; I will update this guide and our Best Kindle Accessories guide with my notes as I test.

Why Are Kindles More Expensive Now?

Amazon raised its prices across its product categories, including Kindle devices. The price increases hit several current Kindle models, leaving only the recent Kindle Scribe models with the original price tag. Amazon declined to comment to WIRED, but a spokesperson told CNET the price hikes were due to rising costs in memory and storage components. It's interesting that none of the more powerful Scribe models needed a price update, but it's also a relief since all three of those models are significantly more expensive than a regular Kindle.

Here are all the increases, including Signature versions:

  • Amazon Kindle (2024, 11th Gen): $150 (up $40)
  • Amazon Kindle Paperwhite (2024, 12th Gen): $200 (up $40)
  • Amazon Kindle Paperwhite Signature (2024, 12th Gen): $250 (up $50)
  • Amazon Kindle Colorsoft: $290 (up $40)
  • Amazon Kindle Colorsoft Signature: $320 (up $40)
  • Amazon Kindle Kids (2024, 2nd Gen): $180 (up $50)
  • Amazon Kindle Colorsoft Kids: $300 (up $30)

If you have your eyes on one of these Kindles, I'd wait until Amazon Prime Day or Black Friday to shop when they're on sale. It's likely the sale prices will only bring the Kindle down to the price it was before, but better than paying more.

What About the New Kindle Scribes?

Kindle has three new Kindle Scribes that launched between late 2025 and June 2026. There are now the Kindle Scribe ($500), Kindle Scribe Colorsoft ($630), and the Kindle Scribe Without Front Light ($430). All three have a similar design and software experience, though the Scribe Colorsoft has a color screen and a shorter battery life—only eight weeks of reading time, compared to 12 weeks on the $500 Scribe and an impressive 16 weeks on the Scribe Without Front Light. Like the second-generation model, they're a great choice for note-takers and students, especially with the long battery life, but I still prefer the second-generation's price point.

All three models have a new, taller design with an 11-inch screen, a slightly slimmer form factor, and an updated stylus. They both also have a quad-core chip, a new homepage, and will support a variety of AI features, including AI search (along with some AI tools for summarizing books you're reading without giving spoilers, though those won't arrive until next year). Users can connect to Google Drive and Microsoft OneDrive to mark up documents, which the older model can't do.

Overall, I'd say they're good devices, but as long as the cheaper second-generation Kindle Scribe is available, I think it's the better buy. It has some AI capabilities but no AI search, and has a different homepage design that matches a classic Kindle rather than the notebook-forward design the new ones have. Amazon said it'll get the same homepage this year, but I haven't seen it so far. I'm disappointed these new devices are so much more expensive; at that price, you might as well shop reMarkable's line of digital notebooks and get better features and accessories.

Accessories for Easier Reading

If you've ever had a long reading session that gives you hand cramps, these accessories might help. You can check out more options in our Best Kindle Accessories guide.

Cases and Covers

Amazon Kindles are, thankfully, not as fragile as a pricey smartphone, but you may still want to add a cover to protect the screen if you're frequently toting it around in a bag. These aren't padded for serious drops, but they are some of the best Kindle cases I've found for daily protection from scratches and scuffs. Also, don't forget that the Kids' editions come with cases, so if you're buying one of those, you won't need a case.

About Those Older Kindles

Amazon doesn't release new Kindles often—the company usually takes a few years between models. Whenever a new one arrives, its predecessor's stock starts to dwindle. It's not that we don't recommend these per se, but I only suggest these if you can find them on sale for the right price. And don't buy too old a model, since Amazon has started pulling support for older Kindles.

Before making your purchase, cross-check the price against the latest model to make sure you're paying a fair amount less for the older device.

Kindle (2022, 11th Generation): This is the smallest of the lot at 6.2 inches tall and 4.3 inches wide, with a 6-inch screen. If you find tablets too cumbersome to hold with one hand, consider this one. With this model, Amazon doubled the storage to 16 gigabytes and upgraded the display to 300 pixels per inch (PPI) resolution (up from 167 PPI). It's tough to find, and I usually don't see it for less than $75 these days.

Kindle Paperwhite (2021, 11th Generation): This is the next step up from the basic model. It has a bright 6.8-inch screen with adjustable warm lighting, a fast page-turn rate, a USB-C port, and 16 gigs of storage. It's waterproof too. We like the Signature Edition, which also includes auto-adjust brightness and 32 gigabytes of storage. Don't recommend spending more than $100 if you can find them.

Kindle Scribe (1st Generation): The original Scribe is a great option for note-takers. It has a giant 10.2-inch screen for taking notes, marking up PDFs, or drawing, and numerous paper formats you can choose, like college-ruled or dotted. It also comes with the Basic Pen, which feels natural to write with and attaches to the side of the Scribe magnetically. It's only worth it for $230 or less, and I often see it for under $200 on eBay.

Kindle Kids (2022): This is an older kid-friendly model. It comes with a cover, a year’s subscription to Amazon Kids+, parental controls, and a two-year warranty, but the fact that it's only available secondhand means you'll likely miss out on the subscription window and may or may not still have a cover. Ideally, don't spend more than $70 on this one.

Kindle Paperwhite Kids (2021): This older Paperwhite version is a step up from the previous basic Kids models. It has a high-resolution 300-ppi display with an adjustable warm screen and is also waterproof. You shouldn't spend more than $110 on this one.

FAQs

Which Kindle Models Lost Amazon Support and Kindle Store Access?

As of May 20, 2026, Amazon stopped supporting Kindles released in 2012 or earlier. That means these models will not be able to get new books through Amazon's services or be registered to an Amazon account. You will be able to read books already on the device, though, and can manually download documents and books via USB cable and via software like Calibre.

The following Kindle devices are impacted:

  • Kindle 1st Generation
  • Kindle 2nd Generation
  • Kindle DX
  • Kindle DX Graphite
  • Kindle Keyboard (3rd Generation)
  • Kindle 4
  • Kindle Touch
  • Kindle 5
  • Kindle Paperwhite 1st Generation

What’s the Best Way to Buy or Sell an Older Kindle?

Have an old Kindle lying around? Are you looking at a used one for sale? If you're trying to figure out what model it is, this Amazon page includes photos, specs, and release years for the entire lineup. Once you know which one you have, you may be able to trade it in for credit toward a newer model.

Most old Kindles probably still work, just with fewer bells and whistles. It's best to avoid Kindles with keyboards or any other physical buttons other than page-turn buttons. Some older models lost the ability to browse, purchase, or borrow new books directly from the device. However, you'll still be able to do this via Amazon on your computer or phone and have it sent to your Kindle, which is a better experience anyway. These models include the Kindle 2nd Generation (International), Kindle DX International, Kindle DX Graphite, Kindle Keyboard, Kindle 4th Generation, and Kindle 5th Generation.

How Do You Get Free Ebooks on a Kindle?

If you buy every single book you want to read on a Kindle, it can add up! But there are ways to save some money while reading as much as your heart desires. You may want to subscribe to Kindle Unlimited for $12 a month. You can only choose from the Unlimited catalog, but there are millions of titles there, including audiobooks and magazines. Start out with the 30-day free trial.

If you already pay for a Prime account, you're eligible for some free ebooks through Prime Reading. There are not as many options as with Kindle Unlimited, and in a lot of cases, you'll see both Unlimited and Prime options lumped together; you'll have to look closely to find the free ebooks. It's still something, and there are even a few magazines.

If you don't want another monthly subscription and don't want to continue giving your money to Amazon, take advantage of the ebooks available with your library card. Browsing a digital catalog is not as magical as spending an afternoon looking over every shelf in a library, but such is the ebook life (no one says you can't read both!). We have a detailed how-to on this that you should check out, but here are some of the takeaways:

  • Get a library card for your local branch.
  • Check your branch's website for its ebook offerings. Many libraries use a service called OverDrive.
  • Download directly to your Kindle library. They'll automatically be removed when they're due back.

If you know someone else with a Kindle, you can lend books between your libraries, just as you would with a physical copy. Follow these instructions from Amazon if you want to share an ebook, but keep in mind that not all books can be loaned.

What Else Can a Kindle Do?

Kindles have helpful features you may want to take advantage of. Long-press a word or phrase to see its definition, highlight it, or take notes. You can also search the entire book for that particular word or phrase or translate it to or from other languages.

Word Wise shows short definitions in small text within the lines. Unfortunately, it's not available for all books, but when it is, you can turn it on or off and choose more and fewer hints. Clicking the short definition opens a longer one from Word Wise and the New Oxford American Dictionary or Oxford Dictionary of English (you can switch between the two), plus translations and a Wikipedia page, if applicable.

While reading, tap the top of the screen and click “Aa” to change font size or type—there's even a font called OpenDyslexic that helps make reading easier for people with dyslexia. You can control margin sizes and line spacing from that menu too.

When a Kindle is connected to a Bluetooth speaker or headphones, VoiceView Screen Reader (accessed through Settings > Accessibility) allows you to use gestures to navigate your device and reads aloud what you've pressed. It will also read a book aloud, though it doesn't sound nearly as nice as an audiobook.

Amazon owns Goodreads, so it syncs seamlessly to Kindles (press the three-dot menu > Goodreads). If you have a Goodreads account, you can review the Kindle books you've read or browse your bookshelf and recommendations. Long-pressing a word or phrase, in addition to what is mentioned above, opens up an option to share quotes directly to Goodreads.

There's a web browser too if you're connected to the internet (three-dot menu > Web Browser). It's not the best, so I'd reserve it for emergency searches.

How Do You Update a Kindle?

When Amazon releases a new software update, it will download and install to your Kindle automatically when it's connected to Wi-Fi. You can check if you're on the latest software by going to Settings > Device Options > Advanced Options > Update Your Kindle. If it's not on the latest software version, you'll see an update available and the Kindle will then prompt you to download and install it.

What Do I Do If My Kindle Colorsoft Has a Yellow Bar?

Following customer complaints in 2024 of a yellow bar at the bottom of the Colorsoft Signature’s screen and discoloration along the edges, an Amazon spokesperson confirmed to WIRED that "customers who notice this can reach out to our customer service team for a replacement or refund.” The company also said it’s “making the appropriate adjustments to ensure that new devices will not experience this issue moving forward.” However, there are still customer complaints about this issue, even with the new model out. We have not run into this issue while testing the Colorsoft, Colorsoft Signature, or Scribe Colorsoft.

Is This a Good Time to Buy a Kindle?

The best time to buy a Kindle is during a major sale event like Amazon Prime Day or Black Friday, because Amazon often has steep discounts. Amazon has always had sales on some (if not all) of its Kindles on past Amazon Prime Day and similar events, like Amazon Big Deal Days.

You can also wait for other sale events if you're not ready to shop yet. Kindles are often on sale for Black Friday and Cyber Monday, which will occur in late November. Other sales often happen from time to time, but these sale events have consistent Kindle deals, so they're a good time to wait for if you want a better price.

Are Kindles Good for Students?

Kindles are great for students, though the model they'll like best will vary on how they use it. If they want to pair it with a stylus for highlighting and be able to take notes, get a Kindle Scribe model. These models also have long battery life, making them great for students to use for weeks on end without worrying about charging. You can get some textbooks on a Kindle too, and send library books to them. For students who love to read but don't want to take a ton of notes, a regular Kindle or Kindle Paperwhite will be best for them.
