entries.title: Amazon Kindle, Paperwhite, and Colorsoft 2026: Specs, Price, Release Date
entries.summary: Ahead of the Kindle’s 20th anniversary next year, Amazon is refreshing its entire range of e-readers with fresh colors, an aluminum build, and a new frame design that’s both thinner and lighter.
entries.content:
The Kindle will turn 20 in 2027. Amazon says it plans to celebrate the milestone throughout the year, but to kick things off, it's starting with an entirely refreshed Kindle lineup.

On Thursday, the company introduced a handful of new Kindle models: a new 6-inch base Kindle, a 7-inch Kindle Paperwhite, and a 7-inch Kindle Colorsoft. You can buy Signature Editions of the latter two and Kids versions of the entire range, which include artist-designed kids cases, a year of Amazon's worry-free guarantee for damage, and a year of Kids+, the company's subscription service that offers unlimited access to ad-free, child-appropriate books.

The highlight is Amazon's use of aluminum for the Kindle's construction rather than traditional plastic. The starting tier is plastic, but you can upgrade to an all-aluminum model (Amazon uses 80 percent recycled aluminum) if you prefer that Kindle model and you just want something more robust.

It can get a little confusing with all the different SKUs, so here's a quick rundown:

Lighter and Premium

The base Kindle, the aluminum version, and the Kids Kindle are on sale starting today. The Paperwhite and Colorsoft are available for preorder on a rolling basis and will launch at the end of October.

The Kindle's screen offers 30 percent faster book opening than its predecessor, Amazon says. The build is a whole millimeter thinner at 6.8 mm, and Amazon cut the weight by around 18 grams to 140 grams. The Kindle Paperwhite and Colorsoft are both similarly lighter (204 grams) and thinner (6.8 mm), retain the waterproof design, and feature adjustable warm reading lights. Like before, the screen has a higher pixel density that makes text appear sharper.

Amazon says the new Kindles are also compliant with the European Union’s new battery regulations, meaning the batteries should be easier to remove and replace.

Upgrading to the Signature Edition for the Colorsoft and Paperwhite nets you the aluminum build, an ambient light sensor that adjusts brightness automatically, and an accelerometer that lets you turn the screen to landscape orientation and have the pages adjust accordingly. The upgrade also adds the ability to use a double-tap gesture to turn pages.

Uniquely, the Signature Editions feature pogo pins that let you charge via Amazon's new $60 dock, which props the device up as it charges. There's also a new Page-Turn Cover ($80)—a case with physical page-turn buttons that magnetically attaches to the back of the devices and pairs via the pogo pins, which Amazon says offers page-turn buttons to the vocal minority that still loves them (around 5 percent of Kindle users) without adding unnecessary bulk to the device.

Don't worry, you don't need the case, the Signature Edition, or even a new Kindle if you just want page-turn buttons. Amazon is debuting its own Kindle Click, a $35 page-turn accessory that pairs over Bluetooth for the non-Signature (and older) Kindle models.

Kindle Ablaze

The Kindle business is booming. Amazon's Kevin Keith, vice president of devices, says Kindles have seen double-digit growth over the last three years, with 2025 being the highest sales year in more than a decade. He says 60 to 65 percent of people buying new devices have never had a Kindle before, with Gen Z, millennials, and even Gen Alpha driving the lion's share. This past January saw the highest single-month Kindle reading volume in history.

At the same time, Kindles are more expensive than ever. “Memory pricing is a little bit crazy,” Keith says, referring to the memory shortage behind the general price bump on all electronics. Amazon upped prices of existing Kindles earlier this year; the new devices match those prices.

Part of the redesign aims to lower overall manufacturing costs and standardize the hardware. Take the refreshed display on the base Kindle—Keith says many of the improvements trickle down from the development of the Kindle Scribe. For the first time, the base Kindle has a display that sits flush with the body, just like its pricier counterparts. (It previously had a raised plastic bezel around the screen.) That whole front panel is also available in a new color: Ube (purple).

While Amazon has made Kindles with colorful fronts (like the matcha green Kindle from 2024), it hasn't done this with flush displays. That's because simply coloring the front would make the Ube color, for example, scatter around the screen as the frontlight reflects it, casting a purple hue on the display. To counter this, Keith says Amazon developed a new “edge-to-edge” color technology that prints two different colors under the cover lens: the Ube color backed by a layer of black. The black absorbs the light, which solves the problem. Amazon says it perfected this tech in the Scribe and ported it down here.

Color is important. Keith says alternative colors typically make up just 15 to 20 percent of sales—the rest being classic options like black or white—but the matcha green model captured a surprising 55 percent. Amazon also chose that color because, at the time, it noticed a general increase in the popularity of matcha in drinks and sweets (it also noted that folks on #BookTok are reading in coffee shops). Hence the new ube color, which is based on the popular purple yam of the same name.

“We've been tracking food trends, and two years ago, ube just exploded—ube was growing 200 percent year over year,” says Chris Green, Amazon's vice president of design. “We expect it to do far better than the matcha.”

For the aluminum housing, instead of milling the device's frame from a block of aluminum and using a lot of water in the process, Amazon stamps a flat sheet, which then goes into a forge that presses down to create the backplate and sides. The process supposedly takes seconds compared to the hours it can take to machine a single aluminum device frame (like an iPhone or MacBook), saving material and energy. It helps lower the Kindle's carbon footprint, which is now equivalent to 11 hardcover books.

Green says these improvements bring down the device's density. The density of the average human body is around 1 gram per cubic centimeter; an iPhone is around 2.2 grams per cubic centimeter. The new Kindles are around 1.2 grams. Lowering that number can help make the hardware “disappear” during prolonged use.

“I truly want people to never think about the Kindle,” Green says. “I just want them to think about the magical world that the author has created inside of this device.”

For Green, who has designed nearly all of Amazon's hardware in his 19-year tenure at the company (and yes, he says he's embarrassed by the Fire Phone), chasing that 1.2-grams-per-cubic-centimeter target is all about getting the gadget out of the way so the Kindle can mimic the analog calm of physical print.

“More people are reading on paper, more people are reading on Kindles,” Green says. “Is it a backlash to AI? Probably. People are trying to find things more authentic—we're in a crisis of authenticity.” Surveys have shown that overall leisure reading is down across the US, but the people who are reading are buying more than ever.

As for the 20th anniversary of the Kindle in 2027, Keith says the company may roll out a significant refresh to the Kindle's user interface, though he didn't share more. Expect special anniversary editions of some Kindles. When I asked whether we could expect the return of the Kindle Oasis—an asymmetrical e-reader with physical page-turn buttons—Green chuckles.

“The first Oasis was one of my passion projects,” he says. “I loved that. I really, really loved that product. But I was a vocal minority on that—most of the people wanted slabs.”

So, probably not.

Correction on October 1, 2026 at 2:30 pm: We've updated this story to correct an incorrect statement about page-turn speed that Amazon initially provided (along with Kevin Keith's title).

entries.title: The Best Early Amazon Echo Deals (and the Worst) Ahead of Prime Big Deal Days
entries.summary: Amazon raised prices across its devices in August. Here are the early device deals ahead of Prime Day that are still worth it—and which aren’t.
entries.content:
Amazon's Prime Day has returned for its fall edition, and the Amazon Alexa-powered devices are already on sale. But are the sales actually any good?

There's already the question of whether you want Alexa in your house, and now it's a question of whether the sales are more of a mind game than a real discount. That's thanks to Amazon raising prices across its device categories at the end of August, leaving us with the same product lineup but a worse case to recommend it. Some devices are already on sale right now ahead of Amazon's Prime Big Deal Days for $40 off, but went up in price by $20 just a few weeks ago, cutting that discount into something that feels barely worth the spend.

If you're interested in Amazon's device sales but want the real picture of what the discount is and which devices are worth it, I've got you covered. I've been testing Amazon Alexa speakers since they launched in 2012, and I am also WIRED's resident Kindle tester, which gives me almost too much insight into the price games Amazon plays with these devices. Here's my full breakdown.

Which Amazon Devices Are on Sale Already, and Which Aren’t

Right now, Amazon's Alexa-powered Echo speakers and Fire TV sticks are currently on sale ahead of Amazon Prime Big Deal Days next week (October 6-7). These devices saw price hikes at the end of August, so some of the deals aren't as good as in the past. They do seem to be permanent price changes, though, so if you're certain you want one of these models, this is the best time to buy.

So far, most Kindles aren't on sale yet, but all three Kindle Kids models (the Kindle Kids, the Kindle Paperwhite Kids, and Kindle Colorsoft Kids) are already on sale. (Amazon also announced new versions of these Kindles today, along with the rest of its lineup, so it's up to you whether you want the current on-sale model or to preorder the new one!) If you're looking for a Paperwhite and Scribe, they aren't on sale yet as of this writing. Neither are Eero routers.

But I expect most of those models will be discounted once the event begins. Both Kindle and Eero products also saw price hikes at the end of August, so I recommend buying them only on sale (even if the sales aren't as good as they used to be, since they're similar discounts but on higher prices).

The Best Early Amazon Device Deals

Not all deals are great, especially given the recent price increases. If you're set on getting a new Amazon Alexa-powered speaker, though, here are the discounts (and devices themselves!) that are still worth it.

The Best Early Kindle Deals

If you're shopping for a Kindle, this is the best time to buy since most were hit with price increases. You won't get as good a deal anymore, but it's much better to buy it at a discount on the new price than the full, higher price for the same product. There's also new Kindles that were just announced, so it's up to you if you want to grab an older on-sale model (which all work great!) or wait for the new one.

As of this writing, only Kindle Kids models are on sale ahead of Amazon Prime Big Deal Days, but only one is a good deal after taking the price changes into account.

Other On-Sale Amazon Devices We’ve Tested

Looking for a different device during Amazon's sale event? We've tested several other Amazon Echo and Fire TV devices that are also on sale right now. Here's what else you can consider, and what the discount looks like.

  • Amazon Echo Dot Max for $80 ($40 Off): If you're looking for a small speaker with bigger sound than the older Echo Dot, the Echo Dot Max has impressive sound for its size, plus a built-in smart home hub. Its price did increase $20, though, so it feels like it's just $20 off even if it looks like $40.
  • Amazon Echo Show 8 (4th Gen) for $125 ($75 Off): While this model is on sale, I prefer the older Echo Show 8 (though it seems rarely available anymore) and the Echo Show 11 since both have better sound. It's a good discount, even off the original $180 price tag, but I'd just spend $25 more and get the better Echo Show 11 if you're set on a new Amazon Alexa-powered smart display.
  • Amazon Echo Show 15 for $250 ($100 Off): The Echo Show 15 and Echo Show 21 are on sale and both double as a Fire TV device, with a massive screen, a flat back for mounting, and an included Alexa Voice Remote. I don't love the TV experience, but it works, and the homepage fits a ton of widgets if you want to see multiple at once. Both sizes are discounted, but both models also cost more now, so it's not as good as you'd think for the same device.
  • Amazon Fire TV Stick 4K Max for $45 ($40 Off): If you love Amazon Prime as your streaming service, this is the favorite we've tested of Amazon's Fire TV streaming devices. It's not a crazy discount since it went up $25 in August, but it's still a really affordable streaming stick during this same event.
  • Amazon Kindle Paperwhite Kids for $170 ($60 Off): The Paperwhite Kids has everything we like about a Kindle Paperwhite, but adds a cover to protect it from any drops by your kiddo's hands and comes with six months of Kids+ content, which is like Kindle Unlimited but designed for kids. It's a good device, but the discount isn't as good as before; it used to retail for $180, so it's really only $10 off what it used to cost. But you won't find it new for cheaper.
  • Amazon Kindle Kids for $123 ($57 Off): This is the cheapest Kindle Kids device, with a 6-inch screen similar to the cheapest Kindle, and it still comes with a colorful cover and six months of Kids+ content like the Paperwhite Kids above. It has the smallest discount out of the Kids devices, and it used to retail for $130, so it's only $7 off the original price. The other Kids models are a better buy.

Which Amazon Device Prices Went Up?

Amazon raised prices across several of its device categories at the end of August. It's not a shocking move, but it hit many affordable products and makes for a worse sale season since we're getting discounts on a higher price tag for no other improvements. Here's a quick breakdown of most of the price changes to help you navigate what sales are good and which are really just bringing you back to the old price.

Either way, I'd only buy an Amazon device on sale now, but it is unfortunate the sales just won't be as good anymore on these existing devices. I expect most, if not all, of these devices to go on sale at some point during Amazon Prime Big Deal Days.

The Amazon Echo smart speaker price changes were:

  • Echo Dot (5th Gen): $80 (up $30)
  • Echo Spot (2nd Gen): $110 (up $30)
  • Echo Dot Max: $120 (up $20)
  • Echo Show 5 (3rd Gen): $100 (up $10)
  • Echo Show 8 (4th Gen): $200 (up $20)
  • Echo Show 11: $250 (up $30)
  • Echo Show 15: $350 (up $50)
  • Echo Show 21: $500 (up $100)

The Amazon Kindle e-reader price changes were:

  • Amazon Kindle (2024, 11th Gen): $150 (up $40)
  • Amazon Kindle Paperwhite (2024, 12th Gen): $200 (up $40)
  • Amazon Kindle Paperwhite Signature (2024, 12th Gen): $250 (up $50)
  • Amazon Kindle Colorsoft: $290 (up $40)
  • Amazon Kindle Colorsoft Signature: $320 (up $40)
  • Amazon Kindle Kids (2024, 2nd Gen): $180 (up $50)
  • Amazon Kindle Colorsoft Kids: $300 (up $30)

The Amazon Eero mesh Wi-Fi routers we recommend saw price changes of:

  • Amazon Eero 7: $400 (up $50)
  • Amazon Eero 7 Pro: $800 (up $100)

And finally, the changes to Fire TV devices we recommend were:

  • Fire TV Stick 4K Max: $85 (up $25)
  • Fire TV Stick HD: $40 (up $5)

entries.title: 2 Driverless Cars Crashed Going 155 mph. That Could Be a Good Thing
entries.summary: Only two of five vehicles finished the race around a notoriously difficult Formula 1 track, exposing what happens when autonomous systems meet blind corners, sensor failures, and physics.
entries.content:
The grandstands erupted with shock as engineers clutched their heads in the paddock. One driverless race car, produced by the company PoliMove, slammed into Unimore’s slowing vehicle in an event held by the Abu Dhabi Autonomous Racing League (A2RL).

At the famous racing track in Imola, Italy, Autodromo Internazionale Enzo e Dino Ferrari, both cars crashed in an area called Rivazza. This is the circuit’s final sequence, made up of corners that are notoriously difficult to navigate. Formula 1 champions have met a similar fate here. But this time, the impact posed no danger to the drivers because there weren’t any.

Launched in 2024, A2RL sought to introduce self-driving cars to the motorsport to test the boundaries of their current capabilities. And this year’s race at Imola revealed those edges, demonstrating the gap between the computational abilities of autonomous vehicles and their capacity to respond when something goes wrong.

Only two of the five cars in the final completed the race. The UAE’s Kinetiz finished first, followed by Germany’s Constructor Racing. PoliMove clocked in at third place, though its battered entrant had to be replaced for the podium ceremony. Two-time winner TUM withdrew its car after it developed a brake problem during the formation lap.

Participating teams had just nine days of physical testing before the race, in conditions that included rain and hail. This also happened to be the league’s first international competition away from its usual testing ground at Abu Dhabi’s Yas Marina Circuit.

So why choose one of motorsport’s most unforgiving tracks?

“Because everybody can do ‘easy’, right?” says Nicola Palarchi, engineering director at Aspire, the company that founded A2RL. “We have to show we go where it matters.”

Palarchi made it abundantly clear that autonomous racing did not intend to compete with human racing, which would remain its own motorsport. It could even support the latter.

Because autonomous racing is pitched as more than spectacle: It’s a laboratory with guardrails. Its proponents describe it as a way to test perception, prediction, and vehicle control at extreme speeds without endangering a human driver. These are all factors in the safety of driverless cars in the real world, and so measuring the limits at which these vehicles succeed—or perhaps more importantly fail—can inform future improvements in the technology.

The first hurdle is perception. The vehicle’s sensors identify its location and surroundings, informing planning software that then chooses a trajectory. Finally, the control system translates that decision into steering, acceleration, and braking. Racing makes each of these stages more challenging, since at high speeds, vehicles have less time to interpret incomplete information, predict another car’s movements, and execute an evasive maneuver.

“The car will be blind for a certain point because the track drops off,” Alexander Winkler, A2RL’s head of sporting, said before the final. If one vehicle stopped beyond that drop, he explained, the car behind could have less than a second to react.

That warning proved prescient.

Unimore said its car, Gianna, initiated a safety stop after losing all data from its lidar and radar sensors. GPS alone could not locate the car accurately enough to continue racing at speed. The team said future systems could use cameras and an inertial measurement unit to continue at a slower pace until precise localization returned. In other words, the car stopped because it lacked a reliable fallback.

PoliMove’s vehicle, Eva, detected Gianna ahead, according to the team, but could not avoid hitting it. Gianna had braked with a force of approximately 1 g, with Eva just 1.5 seconds behind it.

PoliMove said its system identified the danger and began an evasive maneuver. But perception, decisionmaking, trajectory replanning, actuator response, and vehicle dynamics all introduce delays. Once Gianna braked that severely mid-corner, the team said, a collision was physically impossible to avoid.

Even F1 legends like Fernando Alonso and Carlos Sainz have crashed at this part of the track. However, the A2RL teams’ explanation exposes a problem that faster processors alone cannot solve: An autonomous vehicle may recognize a hazard and still be unable to respond before physics takes over.

TUM’s failure was less algorithmic but equally instructive. The team said its car, Hailey, retired after the rear-left brake became stuck at low-to-medium pressure during the formation lap. Even sophisticated autonomous software cannot compensate for mechanical faults.

Kinetiz’s car, Sparkz, took the lead all the way to a first-place podium finish with Constructor AI’s vehicle as the runner-up. But almost any result can be considered progress when the failures produce useful edge cases: sensor loss, compromised localization, sudden braking, limited visibility, and interaction between autonomous systems making separate decisions.

Beyond crash data, Palarchi says these motorsport environments provide the opportunity to develop more resilient hardware. Temperatures in cockpits can get near 170 degrees F, and—while hopefully your robotaxi is not that hot—radars and lidars that can withstand high heat can be useful in our warming cities.

Chee Kiong Ong, deputy team principal at Kinetiz, also observes that predictive algorithms developed on the track could eventually help civilian vehicles respond to emergencies. “You could probably apply it to make the car stop itself in a safer manner or control it at the limits so that you can save lives,” he says.

One caveat is that, unlike other lab testing, the companies aren’t required to share the precise data collected from their vehicles. The data from A2RL’s EAV 25, the racing car developed by the league based on modified Dallara SF23 cars, currently stays within the competition.

The next A2RL race returns to Yas Marina, where teams have spent years developing their software. Organizers are already considering making the competition harder by shortening testing periods, increasing the grid to eight cars, or restricting access to GPS.

Those changes could reveal whether the systems are becoming more adaptable. In the meantime, we’ll wait to see how this information transfers into real-life scenarios.

This story originally appeared in WIRED Middle East.

entries.title: Measles Is Forcing Hospitals to Adapt to a New Normal
entries.summary: The US resurgence of measles is forcing hospitals and health systems to adopt new protocols and procedures to deal with a disease they thought was in the past.
entries.content:
John Goldman had not seen a case of measles in 30 years. But since April, the infectious disease specialist with the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center in central Pennsylvania has had dozens of patients come down with the disease.

“I never thought I would see this come back,” he says.

His health system, like others, has had to adapt to a new normal as measles makes a comeback in the United States. As the country’s cases top 3,600, the highest yearly total since 1991, hospitals and health care providers are being forced to dust off decades-old protocols or develop new ones to deal with the highly contagious disease.

The University of Pittsburgh Medical Center’s community hospital in Lititz is in Lancaster County, the center of Pennsylvania’s current outbreak. It has evaluated around 50 patients with measles, with roughly 20 of those requiring hospitalization. Statewide, Pennsylvania has recorded 943 cases, including 176 hospitalizations and five measles-related deaths as of September 30.

Goldman says the Lititz hospital has rapidly ramped up measles screening, asking patients if they are experiencing symptoms such as fever, cough, sore throat, red eyes, and whether they are vaccinated. The classic measles rash does not appear until three to five days after these cold-like symptoms begin, or about one to two weeks after exposure to the virus.

The hospital is instructing physicians to call ahead before referring a patient with suspected measles to the emergency department. Patients must wear a mask and wait in the parking lot, where a staff member meets them and escorts them directly to a negative-pressure room, bypassing the waiting area. These special isolation spaces have lower air pressure than outside hallways, which traps airborne pathogens inside and prevents them from spreading within a hospital. Patients who don’t have serious symptoms are asked to stay at home.

“We are really trying to prevent people from coming to the hospital with measles, because once they’re in the hospital, it's very easy for them to expose other people,” Goldman says.

Jennifer Janco, chair of pediatrics for St. Luke’s University Health Network, which serves eastern Pennsylvania and New Jersey, says that with falling vaccination rates and increasing measles cases around the country, “it was only a matter of time before we started seeing cases.”

St. Luke’s treated two unvaccinated siblings for measles in late July. One of the siblings was hospitalized in a different health network but released, and both were able to recover at home while pediatricians oversaw their care remotely. The health network has also tested other patients suspected of having measles.

To prepare for possible measles cases, Janco says the health system stocked up on the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine, as well as immune globulin, a mix of antibodies derived from healthy human blood plasma. The MMR vaccine can prevent infection or make the illness milder if given within 72 hours of initial measles exposure for people who haven’t been vaccinated, and immune globulin can be given up to six days after exposure to help ease symptoms.

Deploying those interventions requires quick, accurate testing. Because measles was rare for so long, most hospitals do not have the ability to test in-house for the disease. Instead, a nasal or throat swab is collected and sent to a commercial or state public health laboratory. The turnaround time for results is one to three days.

“There’s a narrow window of time to offer prevention for exposed, vulnerable people,” Janco says.

Janco says in cases where measles is highly likely—for example, if the patient is unvaccinated and had exposure to an infected person—the Pennsylvania Department of Health will send a representative to collect a patient sample at their home. In other instances, patients have been asked to wait in their car in the parking lot, where a health care provider meets them and collects a sample to avoid exposing others.

When measles cases began appearing in Spartanburg County, South Carolina, last fall, staff at Prisma Health in nearby Greenville started discussing how they would handle measles cases if the outbreak got bigger.

“Since Covid, we haven't really had to think a lot about how we flow patients through a system, or the special things that we need to have in place to really protect not only the health care givers but also the other patients who are susceptible,” says Robin LaCroix, a pediatric infectious disease physician at Prisma Health.

But the planning proved prescient: A total of 997 cases from October 2025 through March 2026 were tied to an outbreak centered around Spartanburg County and the upstate region in South Carolina.

Newborns are among the most susceptible to measles, since babies don’t usually receive their first dose of the MMR vaccine until 12 months of age. To protect them, the health system asked parents with newborns to call their pediatrician’s office when they arrived for an appointment and enter through a separate door so they didn’t have to sit in a waiting room.

In addition to newborns, immunocompromised and pregnant people are also at higher risk of serious complications from measles. To prevent potential exposures in doctors’ offices, providers started screening patients for measles over the phone when scheduling appointments and in person upon arrival.

Prisma’s Greenville Memorial Hospital, which tested 400 patients for measles during the outbreak and cared for 13 hospitalized patients, didn’t have enough negative-pressure rooms to handle suspected and confirmed cases, so staff had to retrofit regular rooms. That involved bringing in portable air scrubbers and high-efficiency particulate air filters, and at times moving measles patients to a room that didn’t share a common air-handling unit with rooms where non-measles patients were staying. This required the health network’s engineering department to assess ventilation systems and measure airflow to figure out where staff could safely relocate patients.

In urgent care clinics and doctors’ offices without negative pressure capability, a potential measles exposure could be very disruptive to patient care, LaCroix says. Since measles can remain airborne in a space for two hours after an infected person leaves, a room that a suspected measles patient had been in needed to be closed and vacated for that amount of time before it was usable again, causing longer wait times for other patients.

Prisma also tried to keep infected patients out of health care settings if they had milder infections. At the height of South Carolina’s outbreak, the health system relied heavily on telemedicine visits. Some pediatricians were seeing patients twice a day to check in on their status and determine whether they needed to come into the hospital.

Collectively, the measures needed to protect patients from exposure and the changes in workflow were difficult for both patients and staff, LaCroix says.

For many hospitals, measles’ return means heightened vigilance to keep the most vulnerable safe. Geisinger Medical Center in Danville, Pennsylvania, had to update visitation rules to its neonatal intensive care unit in August following a potential measles exposure from a hospital visitor. Now, only a baby’s parents or legal guardians are permitted to visit the NICU, and only if they do not have signs or symptoms associated with measles. Geisinger has since implemented screening of parents and legal guardians for measles symptoms upon entering its Danville facility, and it expanded the protocols to its children’s hospital in early September.

“It is a resource strain,” Janco says. “There are so many pieces that have to fall into place to make sure that we're doing everything we can to contain this.”
